# Winifred

*Storyteller of the Old Quarter*

## Personality

Twinkling, mischievous and endlessly patient with children. She tells the same story differently every time.

## Lore

Winifred is seventy-four, and every evening, when the lamps are lit in the old quarters, she sets a stool on her doorstep in the narrow lane where her husband Simkin mends shoes, folds her hands in her lap and waits. She never has to wait long. Within a few minutes the children arrive, from the lanes and the courtyards and, in her grandson's case, from somewhere above, and she tells them a story. Half the children of the old quarters grew up on Winifred's stories. A good many of their parents did too.

### Where the stories came from

She was born in the old quarters and went to work at twelve for a seamstress who sewed for the envoys' households near the plaza: the Savage halls, the Magician houses, the Commons merchants' widows and the old Aristocrat families who still kept rooms in the capital. Winifred hemmed and pinned and carried, and above all she listened. Every household had its own stories, and every one of them told the Balrog War differently. In the Savage hall she heard of a horned giant wreathed in flame, woken from the deep earth by the noise of the old wars. In the Magician houses she heard of a wound in the world, a hunger come through a tear from somewhere else. The Commons widows called it the Burning and said it had always been under the island. The Aristocrat families showed her chronicles full of armies and burned towns and very little about the thing that burned them.

She kept all four. She has kept them for more than sixty years, and she has added to them from every traveller who ever sat down on her step.

### The same story differently

Winifred is twinkling, mischievous and endlessly patient with children, and she tells the same story differently every time. On Monday the Balrog comes out of the ground; on Thursday it comes out of the sky. In one telling of the Last Stand at the Tree the Savage line holds for three days, in the next for nine. The children argue about it furiously on the way home, which is, she says, the point. She refuses, absolutely and cheerfully, to say which version she believes. When anyone presses her, she says that she believes the one she is telling, for as long as she is telling it.

Lately the questions have changed. The children used to ask whether the Balrog was real. Now, with monsters on the roads and their fathers coming home from the gate with stories of their own, they ask whether it is coming back. Winifred does not know, and she does not pretend to. She tells them that the four peoples beat it once, together, and that the kingdom they made is still here. Then she tells them a funny one, so that they sleep.

### Simkin, Gytha and Hodge

She married Simkin forty-nine years ago, the year after he took the little shop in the lane, and they have argued happily ever since. He is grumpy and chatty and judges people by their soles; she judges them by their stories, and the two methods agree more often than either will admit. Their only child, Gytha, came late, when Winifred was thirty-nine and had stopped expecting her. Gytha talks faster than both her parents put together and runs the washing yard in the courtyard round the corner.

Winifred helps raise Gytha's son, Hodge, who is ten. Hodge's father is the one story Winifred has never told and never asked for. Gytha does not speak of him, and Winifred, who can get a story out of anyone, has decided that some stories belong to the person who carries them.

Hodge's favourite is the Last Stand at the Tree, and he has noticed that she never tells it the same way twice. What he has not noticed is that his grandmother sleeps very little, and sits at her window at dawn, and has seen a small figure cross the ridge of the roof opposite most mornings with something long over its shoulder. She has not told Gytha. She is waiting to see how the story goes.

### Hooks

A quest might begin with a traveller on Winifred's step telling a fifth version of the Balrog's coming, one she has never heard, and Winifred wanting very much to know where it came from. Or it might begin with Winifred deciding that her grandson's story has reached the part where someone ought to step in.
